item.title: The Mental Trap That Keeps Us Solving the Wrong Problem
item.description:
Cognition

The Mental Trap That Keeps Us Solving the Wrong Problem

How fixed thinking keeps us stuck in the same solutions.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • How we define a problem can hide better solutions.
  • Expertise can lock us into assumptions that once made us successful.
  • Real innovation starts by questioning the problem, not perfecting the same answer.
Source: Shlomo Assa / Used With Permission

I'm sure you can relate to having the same argument again and again. You explain yourself differently, try a new approach, but somehow end up right back where you started. Maybe you've stayed in a job long after you knew it wasn't right for you, working harder instead of asking whether effort was ever the problem. It may feel like progress, but you may be working on the wrong problem.

Psychologists call this functional fixedness. Once we define a problem in a certain way, we can stop seeing that definition and begin building solutions around it without questioning the frame. The same pattern can happen in professional fields, where people spend decades chasing the same goal, such as more power, speed, or intensity, simply because it works well enough.

To learn more about this, I spoke with Shlomo Assa, a technology executive who spent more than a decade working within this mindset before recognizing that the problem itself needed to be redefined. His experience offers a firsthand look at how fixed thinking takes hold and how challenging our assumptions can open the door to better solutions.

What Familiarity Hides

Think about anything you've used the same way for years: a spare room that's stayed “the guest room” for a decade, or a budget line nobody questions. Once something becomes associated with one purpose, your mind can stop considering what else it could be used for.

Psychologist Karl Duncker demonstrated this in 1945 in his classic candle problem study. Participants were given a candle, a box of tacks, and matches, and asked to attach the candle to a wall without letting wax drip onto the table. Many struggled to see that the box itself could be used as a platform for the candle because they viewed it primarily as a container for tacks. This shows how familiarity can limit what we see as possible. Once we associate an object with one purpose, it can be difficult to imagine using it in a different way.

Why Expertise Makes It Worse

The people most likely to get stuck this way are often the most experienced in the room, which is the part nobody wants to hear. The more fluent you become in a field's usual questions, the harder it is to notice when the questions themselves are wrong.

For instance, research suggests that expertise can sometimes narrow how we approach problems. When people become deeply familiar with a field, they can become more attached to established ways of thinking, making it harder to consider new perspectives or alternative solutions. Experts call this cognitive entrenchment.

Assa saw this in his career. "You get very good at the questions your industry has agreed to ask," he says. "You're competing on the same measures as everyone else, improving, so it feels like progress. What you're not doing is asking whether the measure is right, because nobody around you is asking either. The people the technology wasn't serving got treated as outside the market, instead of as evidence the approach was wrong."

Breaking the Frame

This bias often works below our awareness, so simply trying to be more open-minded isn't enough. A recent review of over 50 studies on overcoming fixation found the same pattern every time: The techniques that worked all forced a deliberate pause to question assumptions before jumping to solutions.

Assa's approach follows that same principle. His process is to listen, observe, analyze, challenge, understand the need, and then create. He puts challenge before creation on purpose. "You have to attack your own framing before you fall for your own solution," he says. "Otherwise, you'll defend it without realizing it."

For Assa, that meant questioning assumptions that had long shaped laser treatment design. Instead of accepting pain, long recovery times, and the challenges of safely treating darker skin tones as unavoidable trade-offs, he treated them as problems worth solving. Changing the question changed what was possible.

Action Steps

Here are three simple ways to recognize when you're stuck in a fixed way of thinking and open yourself to a different approach:

  1. List what you've stopped questioning: Entrenched problems get reclassified as “just how things are.” Ask yourself what you've learned to tolerate that you once thought should be different.
  2. Name the goal, not the method: If you can't describe what you want without describing how you pursue it, you're still inside the frame. Separate what you want from the way you've always tried to get it.
  3. Ask someone outside your field: An outsider's “obvious” question can expose an assumption your expertise made invisible. Sometimes the person who knows the least about your usual approach can see the possibility you've stopped noticing.

Bottom Line

Functional fixedness isn't about effort or intelligence. Sometimes we get so used to one way of seeing a problem that we stop noticing other possibilities. The next time something isn't working, before trying harder, stop and ask: Am I solving the right problem? Look at the situation from a different angle, question what you've been assuming, and consider what you would try if you weren't limited by the usual approach. Sometimes a small shift in how you define the problem can change what you see as possible.

item.title: Treating Disease vs. Helping People Heal
item.description:
Integrative Medicine

Treating Disease vs. Helping People Heal

Healing is biological, but it's also psychological, social, and deeply human.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Treating disease and promoting healing are not always identical goals.
  • No single profession can address every dimension of recovery alone.
  • Advances in medicine, diagnostics, and AI systems cannot eliminate the human work behind healing.
  • Providers should be asking two questions: how do we treat the disease, and how do we help the person heal.

A physician can successfully treat a disease without helping a person heal.

At first glance, that statement may seem contradictory. Isn't curing disease the same as healing?

Not always.

Imagine two patients who have survived heart attacks and received excellent medical treatment. Their cholesterol levels improve. Their blood pressure is under control. Their cardiac rehabilitation is complete. From a medical standpoint, both have responded well to treatment. Yet only one returns to work with renewed purpose, reconnects with family, adopts healthier habits, and regains confidence in the future. The other lives in constant fear that another heart attack is imminent. He withdraws from activities he once enjoyed, becomes anxious with every new physical sensation, struggles to sleep, and quietly slips into depression.

Both patients received excellent medical care, but their experiences of healing look remarkably different.

The Achievements and Limits of Modern Medicine

Modern medicine has achieved extraordinary success in diagnosing and treating diseases. Advances in pharmaceuticals, surgery, imaging, genetics, and critical care have transformed illnesses that were once fatal into conditions that can often be effectively managed. These successes deserve recognition and celebration. But treating disease and promoting healing are not always identical goals.

Disease describes the pathological processes affecting a person's health. Medical treatment seeks to identify, manage, or correct those processes. Healing, however, describes a broader process occurring within the person.

Treatment may lower blood pressure, remove a tumor, control blood glucose, or reduce pain. Healing encompasses what happens as a person responds and adapts to the experience of illness. It can include restoring a sense of safety after trauma, rebuilding confidence following illness, adapting to life with a chronic condition, reconnecting with relationships, rediscovering meaning, and finding hope in the face of uncertainty.

In other words, healing is not merely a biological process. It is also psychological, social, and deeply human.

The distinction between treatment and healing becomes increasingly important as healthcare shifts from treating acute illness to managing chronic disease.

Diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic pain, obesity, cancer survivorship, and many neurological conditions require patients to do far more than take medication or complete a procedure. People must continually adapt, make decisions, sustain healthy behaviors, cope with uncertainty, and integrate illness into their daily lives. Sometimes they must learn how to live meaningful lives in the presence of symptoms that medicine cannot completely eliminate.

Medicine provides treatment. People still have to live with the condition.

The Role of Psychology in Supporting Healing

This is where psychology becomes indispensable, not as a replacement for medicine, but as an essential partner in helping people truly heal. Psychology helps us understand why two people with the same diagnosis can experience dramatically different recoveries. Resilience, coping, social support, health beliefs, motivation, purpose, and emotional well-being are all elements of healing, and they all influence how people experience illness and respond to treatment. But psychology does more than help us understand these differences. It can also help patients develop more effective ways of coping, change behaviors that influence health, manage fear and uncertainty, strengthen motivation, mobilize sources of support, and adapt to the realities of living with illness.

Consider the two heart attack survivors. Medicine can explain what happened physiologically and what treatments are necessary to reduce the risk of another cardiac event. But those answers alone may not explain why one patient confidently returns to life while the other becomes consumed by fear. To understand that difference, we have to look beneath the disease. We have to understand the person.

The Need for Multidisciplinary Perspectives

Once we recognize that healing involves biological, psychological, and social dimensions, an important implication follows: No single profession can address every dimension of recovery alone.

Physicians bring expertise in diagnosis, disease management, and medical treatment. Psychologists understand behavior, coping, emotion, motivation, and adaptation. Nurses see dimensions of the patient's experience that may emerge during ongoing care and recovery. Social workers understand the environmental, family, financial, and community circumstances that can determine whether even the best treatment plan is realistic. Rehabilitation specialists help people regain function and independence. Pharmacists contribute expertise that helps patients use increasingly complex treatments safely and effectively.

Each profession brings a different perspective to understanding the person. Healing requires connecting those perspectives. This is the promise of integrated care.

Integrated care is sometimes described primarily in structural terms: different professionals working in the same setting, sharing medical records, or coordinating referrals. Those elements are important, but they are not the ultimate purpose.

The True Goal of Integrated Care: Treating the Whole Person

At its best, integrated care represents a different way of thinking about health. It recognizes that a patient cannot be meaningfully divided into a cardiovascular problem, a behavioral problem, a social problem, and an emotional problem. These dimensions interact continuously within the same person.

Integrated care therefore seeks to bring together the expertise necessary to understand and treat the whole person. It does not replace excellent medical treatment. It expands what excellent treatment can accomplish.

Lowering blood pressure matters. Controlling blood glucose matters. Reducing pain matters. Successfully treating cancer matters. But what happens next matters too. Can the patient return to the activities that give life meaning? Can someone with diabetes sustain the daily behaviors necessary to manage the condition? Can a cancer survivor live without every new ache triggering fear of recurrence? Can someone with chronic pain rebuild relationships, regain function, and construct a meaningful life even if some pain remains? These are not secondary outcomes. They are part of healing.

Perhaps this is why some of the most meaningful moments in healthcare rarely involve sophisticated technology. They occur when a physician asks one more question, when a psychologist helps a patient rediscover hope, when a nurse recognizes that fear is masquerading as anger, or when a social worker discovers that a patient cannot follow a treatment plan because there is no reliable transportation to appointments.

That conversation allows us to look beneath the symptoms and better understand the person experiencing them. Sometimes that means asking questions that cannot be answered by a laboratory test, imaging study, or medical history alone:

  • What has this illness taken from you?
  • What are you afraid of?
  • What makes following this treatment difficult?
  • Who is helping you through this?
  • What would getting better actually mean to you?

The answers may reveal grief, fear, isolation, financial strain, family responsibilities, or a loss of identity that would otherwise remain invisible and unaddressed, hindering the healing process. They do not replace medical information. They add the human context needed to understand what this particular person needs to heal. Healthcare will continue to advance. Better medications, more precise diagnostics, increasingly sophisticated technologies, and artificial intelligence will undoubtedly improve our ability to detect and treat disease. But what they will not do is eliminate the human work behind healing.

People will still experience fear when they receive a diagnosis. They will grieve the loss of abilities they once took for granted. They will struggle to change habitual behaviors developed over decades. They will worry about their families, finances, independence, and futures. They will search for meaning when illness changes the lives they imagined for themselves.

Helping people navigate those experiences requires more than medical expertise alone. It requires psychological understanding, human connection, and healthcare systems designed around the whole person. It has always been a shared endeavor.

Medicine brings tools to diagnose and treat disease. Psychology brings expertise in behavior, coping, adaptation, and meaning. Nursing supports patients throughout illness and recovery. Social work addresses the realities of daily life that influence health. Rehabilitation helps restore function. Families provide connection. Communities foster resilience. Integrated care brings these pieces together around the person who matters most: the patient.

As healthcare continues to evolve, perhaps we should therefore ask two questions rather than one.

  • How do we treat the disease?

And then:

  • How do we help this person heal?

The future of healthcare will not be defined solely by advances in medical treatment or by greater attention to the psychological and human dimensions of health. It will be defined by how effectively we bring these perspectives together.

Treating disease is one of healthcare's greatest achievements. Helping people heal is its greatest purpose.

item.title: Mental Health and Manifestation Culture
item.description:
Media

Mental Health and Manifestation Culture

Spiritual and psychiatric content are symbiotic on social media.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • On social media, astrology content and mental health diagnosis can work similarly (and sometimes together).
  • Our experiences incorporate information from both horoscopes and diagnoses.
  • There is truth to the self-fulfilling prophecy (though it may not make you the luckiest person alive).

“Lucky girl syndrome” was a TikTok trend involving the repeated mental affirmation that one is the luckiest person alive in order to make it so. Explained on social media in terms of neuroscience and spirituality (and sometimes both), this was part of a longer social media trend of manifesting on a platform where it is not uncommon to see users talking about having manifested the very content appearing in their feed.

Media as Mediums and Mental Health Diagnosis as Quasi-Religious

From the telegraph to television to TikTok, communication technologies have suggested access to a realm beyond our senses. Media have been imagined as mediums.

Source: Rob Hampson / Unsplash

There is a long history of humans ascribing to machines the ability not only to tap into unseen dimensions but also into the electrical impulses of our own brains (and today we have the development of brain-to-text technology). The ideas of computers reading our minds did not start with today’s algorithmic social media or AI, but, as Simone Natale writes, have been integral to our cultural imagination around computers since the 1950s and attached to other media technologies for even longer.

Therapy culture, the quest for mental well-being, and psychiatric diagnosis have also been called new forms of spirituality and religion. The DSM has been described as psychiatry’s bible, and not just because it is the go-to professional reference book for diagnosis. Some leading psychiatrists have argued that the DSM has historically leaned more toward revelatory beliefs than scientific evidence. Our contemporary system of psychiatric diagnosis has been hotly disputed since the civil rights era of the 1960s and '70s, as Lucas Richert describes, when psychiatric practitioners, due to the lack of scientific backing, had been likened by critics within the field to witch doctors and shamans.

So when I saw connections between social mental health content and social media astrology content across my research for Mood Disorder, their entanglement perhaps should have been unsurprising, with each being used at times to support and validate the other.

Social Media Manifestations

Take the “lucky girl” notion that what we believe will happen is likely to come to pass. The crucial middle step in this kind of self-fulfilling prophecy is that we not only notice things that align with our beliefs, rejecting other information (confirmation bias), but act in accordance with those beliefs. So, if my students believe they will fail an exam, for example, they may procrastinate studying or feel anxious while taking it, potentially resulting in a lower grade (and reaffirming the initial belief).

In explaining this phenomenon, social media creators easily weave the psychological concept of the self-fulfilling prophecy with the metaphysical concept of manifestation because, while the technical mechanism might vary, the fundamental rule remains: What we pay attention to and what we believe has tangible consequences (maybe not becoming the luckiest person alive, but consequences).

This takes algorithmic form on social media: We all know that what we give our time and attention to online results in increasingly being shown similar content.

There are a lot of other syndromes besides “lucky girl” that people come to identify with through their engagement with social media. Platform users believe social media algorithms can predict everything from whether someone will ghost them to whether they have a mental health disorder.

As concepts of mental disorders shift, our interpretation of our experiences shifts to accommodate those concepts. This change in our subjectivities (how we see ourselves), in turn, affects future conceptualizations. Ian Hacking, a scholar of philosophy of science, called this a “looping effect.” Mental health disorders are not just “discovered” and catalogued forever. They evolve over time. They are revised with social and cultural shifts as much as with psychological research.

Source: Typerium App / Unsplash

Data privacy concerns notwithstanding, there is an enticing aspect to digital media’s ability to tell us something about ourselves (like a delightful end-of-year synopsis of our streaming music taste which, of course, doubles as marketing for the platform when shared).

Importantly, for technologies to work this way, our beliefs about them matter. There are looping effects here too—the algorithm shapes our experience, and our experience then helps shape the algorithm.

Not unlike algorithmic social media feeds that are assumed to calculate something otherwise inaccessible about us, online personality tests offer glimpses into our psyche through popular culture. BuzzFeed quizzes ask which millennial and Gen Z TV characters you are, whether you’re a secret genius or covert narcissist, or, in a particularly memorable one from 2014 that I’ve thought might have been a fever dream but have since verified its existence, “Which Ousted Arab Spring Ruler Are You?”

Some online quizzes are meant to be taken purely as entertainment (dubious as some may be), but others pathologize personality traits and come closer to diagnostic scales of DSM disorders. Not only can these assessments prove less accurate outside of a clinical setting where a practitioner could formulate a detailed case before treatment, but they can amplify mental health misunderstandings.

Part of this stems from our desire to know ourselves and social media’s inherent commodification of that desire. Neither explanation, mathematical nor magical, seems to be adequate in itself to explain or address mental health, which helps account for their blurred boundaries.

All of this also tells me that our mental health supports and frameworks are so profoundly lacking that we continually seek relief through self-pathologizing and oversimplified social media categorizations. Until we expand our ways of considering mental health, we will likely keep taking on any online syndrome as our own, whether from a psychiatrist or a psychic.

Despite both better science and better PR, many argue that diagnostic psychiatry hasn’t gotten a whole lot better since those issues of the 1960s and '70s. There are growing calls for non-diagnostic options for understanding and addressing mental distress and, as I explore in my work, these kinds of frameworks may offer one pathway out of these pathological loops, both in media and mental health.
